## {#learning-obj data-menu-title="Learning Objectives"}

[Learning Objectives]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:

- Use `select()` to keep or remove columns
- Use `mutate()` to change column content and fix data type errors

## {#select-intro data-menu-title="select()"}

[Section 5: `select()` — Keeping What You Need]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
The salmon dataset has two columns we don't need: `All` and 
`notesRegCode`. Use `select()` to keep only what's relevant.
:::

```r
catch_data <- catch_original %>%
    select(Region, Year, Chinook, Sockeye, Coho, Pink, Chum)

head(catch_data)
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
You can also use `select()` to **drop** columns with a minus sign:
:::

```r
catch_data <- catch_original %>%
    select(-All, -notesRegCode)
```

---

## {#quality-check data-menu-title="Quality Check"}

[Section 6: Quality Check with `glimpse()`]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
After selecting, check that everything looks as expected:
:::

```r
dplyr::glimpse(catch_data)
```

```
Rows: 1,708
Columns: 7
$ Region  <chr> "SSE", "SSE", ...
$ Year    <dbl> 1886, 1887, ...
$ Chinook <chr> "0", "0", ...   ← ⚠️ should be numeric!
$ Sockeye <dbl> 5, 155, ...
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
**Chinook is stored as character, not numeric.** This is a common 
problem when data comes from PDFs or Excel files. Let's fix it.
:::

---

## {#mutate-fix data-menu-title="mutate() to fix types"}

[Section 7: Fixing Column Types with `mutate()`]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
`mutate()` creates new columns or overwrites existing ones.

First attempt — convert Chinook to numeric:
:::

```r
catch_clean <- catch_data %>%
    mutate(Chinook = as.numeric(Chinook))
```

```
Warning: NAs introduced by coercion
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
R is telling us it couldn't convert something — let's find out what:
:::

```r
i <- which(is.na(catch_clean$Chinook))
catch_data[i, ]
```

```
  Region  Year Chinook ...
1    GSE  1955 I       ...
```

---

## {#mutate-if-else data-menu-title="mutate() with if_else"}

[Fixing the Data Entry Error]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
The letter `"I"` was misread from a PDF — it should be `"1"`. Use 
`if_else()` inside `mutate()` to fix it before converting:
:::

```r
catch_clean <- catch_data %>%
    mutate(Chinook = if_else(condition = Chinook == "I", 
                             true = "1", 
                             false = Chinook),
           Chinook = as.numeric(Chinook))

## verify the fix
catch_clean[i, ]
```

```
  Region  Year Chinook ...
1    GSE  1955       1 ...
```

:::{.body-text}
This is a realistic data cleaning scenario — real data has real errors.
:::

---

## {#pivot-longer-intro data-menu-title="pivot_longer() intro"}

[Section 8: Reshaping with `pivot_longer()`]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
Our data is currently **wide** — one column per salmon species. For 
most analyses, we want it **long** — one row per observation.
:::

```r
catch_long <- catch_clean %>% 
    pivot_longer(
        cols = -c(Region, Year),
        names_to = "species",
        values_to = "catch"
    )

head(catch_long)
```

```
  Region  Year species catch
1    SSE  1886 Chinook     0
2    SSE  1886 Sockeye  5000
3    SSE  1886    Coho     0
```

---

## {#pivot-longer-explained data-menu-title="pivot_longer() explained"}

[Understanding `pivot_longer()` Arguments]{.slide-title}

```r
pivot_longer(
    cols = -c(Region, Year),   # which columns to pivot
    names_to = "species",      # new column for old column NAMES
    values_to = "catch"        # new column for old column VALUES
)
```

:::{.body-text}
- **`cols`**: the columns being collapsed. Here, everything *except* 
  Region and Year.
- **`names_to`**: the new column that will hold the old column **names** 
  (Chinook, Sockeye, Coho, Pink, Chum → species)
- **`values_to`**: the new column that will hold the old column **values**
:::

---

## {#pivot-wider data-menu-title="pivot_wider()"}

[The Reverse: `pivot_wider()`]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
`pivot_wider()` does the reverse — it spreads rows back out into 
columns. Arguments mirror `pivot_longer()`:
:::

```r
catch_wide <- catch_long %>%
    pivot_wider(names_from = species,
                values_from = catch)

head(catch_wide)
```

```
  Region  Year Chinook Sockeye  Coho  Pink  Chum
1    SSE  1886       0       5     0     0     0
2    SSE  1887       0     155     0     0     0
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
Use `?pivot_longer` and `?pivot_wider` in the console whenever 
you need to remind yourself of the arguments.
:::

---

## {#why-shape-matters data-menu-title="Why Shape Matters"}

[Why Does Shape Matter?]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
The shape of your data determines what operations are possible:

- **Plotting**: `ggplot2` needs data in long format to map species 
  to color aesthetics
- **Modeling**: `lm(catch ~ year)` needs `year` as a column, not 
  column names
- **Summarizing**: `group_by(species)` only works if `species` is a column

**Wide** format → good for data entry, human readability

**Long** format → good for analysis, plotting, modeling
:::

---

## {#rename-intro data-menu-title="rename()"}

[Section 9: `rename()` — Defensive Column Renaming]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
The metadata tells us `catch` values are in **thousands of fish**. 
Let's rename the column before converting:
:::

```r
catch_long <- catch_long %>%
    rename(catch_thousands = catch)
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
**Why use `rename()` instead of `names()[4] <- "catch_thousands"`?**

Using position-based renaming is fragile. If a colleague updates the 
dataset and adds a column, position 4 is now a different column.

`rename()` targets the column **by name** — it breaks loudly if the 
column name changes, and silently adapts if columns are reordered.

This is **defensive coding**.
:::

---

## {#mutate-convert data-menu-title="mutate() to convert units"}

[Section 10: Adding Columns with `mutate()`]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
Now convert from thousands to individual fish, and drop the old column:
:::

```r
catch_long <- catch_long %>%
    mutate(catch = catch_thousands * 1000) %>%
    select(-catch_thousands)

head(catch_long)
```

```
  Region  Year species    catch
1    SSE  1886 Chinook        0
2    SSE  1886 Sockeye     5000
3    SSE  1886    Coho        0
```

:::{.body-text}
Notice: we chained `mutate()` and `select()` together because they're 
part of the same cleaning step.
:::

---

## {#split-apply-combine data-menu-title="Split-Apply-Combine"}

[Section 11: The Split-Apply-Combine Strategy]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
To get average catch per region, we'd "by hand":

1. **Split** — group all rows from the same region together
2. **Apply** — calculate mean catch for each group
3. **Combine** — bring the results into a single table
:::

![](https://nceas-learning-hub.github.io/sfsu_data_sci/images/r_tidyverse_clean_wrangle/regions-split-apply-combine.png){fig-align="center" width="75%"}

---

## {#group-summarize data-menu-title="group_by + summarize"}

[`group_by()` and `summarize()`]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
`dplyr` implements Split-Apply-Combine with two functions:
:::

```r
mean_region <- catch_long %>%
    group_by(Region) %>%
    summarize(mean_catch = mean(catch))

head(mean_region)
```

```
  Region mean_catch
1    ALU    40384.
2    BER    16373.
3    BRB  2709796.
```

:::{.body-text}
- `group_by(Region)` → **splits** by region (invisible grouping)
- `mean(catch)` → **applies** the function to each group
- `summarize()` → **combines** into one row per group
:::

---

## {#count-n data-menu-title="counting rows"}

[Counting Rows per Group]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
Another common use: count the number of rows in each group using 
`n()`:
:::

```r
n_region <- catch_long %>%
    group_by(Region) %>%
    summarize(n = n())
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
**Tip:** The shortcut `count()` does the same thing in one step:
:::

```r
catch_long %>%
    count(Region)
```

---

## {#filter-intro data-menu-title="filter()"}

[Section 12: `filter()` — Keeping Rows by Condition]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
`filter()` keeps rows that match a condition:
:::

```r
sse_catch <- catch_long %>%
    filter(Region == "SSE")
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
You can filter on multiple conditions:
:::

```r
## Chinook from the SSE region only
chinook_sse <- catch_long %>%
    filter(Region == "SSE",
           species == "Chinook")

## catches over one million fish
big_catch <- catch_long %>%
    filter(catch > 1000000)
```

---

## {#arrange-intro data-menu-title="arrange()"}

[Section 13: `arrange()` — Sorting Rows]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
`arrange()` sorts a data frame by one or more columns:
:::

```r
## ascending (default)
mean_region <- catch_long %>%
    group_by(Region) %>%
    summarize(mean_catch = mean(catch)) %>%
    arrange(mean_catch)

## descending
mean_region <- catch_long %>%
    group_by(Region) %>%
    summarize(mean_catch = mean(catch)) %>%
    arrange(desc(mean_catch))
```

:::{.body-text}
Common use cases: displaying sorted tables in reports, calculating 
cumulative sums where row order matters.
:::

---

## {#separate-unite data-menu-title="separate() and unite()"}

[Section 14: `separate()` and `unite()`]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
Split one column into many:
:::

```r
sites_df %>%
    separate(site, c("island", "site_number"), "-")
```

```
  island site_number
1    HAW         101
2    OAH         320
3    MAU         039
```

. . .

:::{.body-text}
Combine many columns into one:
:::

```r
dates_df %>%
    unite(date, year, month, day, sep = "-")
```

```
        date
1 1930-12-14
```

---

## {#all-together data-menu-title="All Together"}

[Section 15: Putting It All Together]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
A complete pipeline — from raw data to result — in a single readable 
expression:
:::

```r
mean_region <- catch_original %>%
  select(-All, -notesRegCode) %>% 
  mutate(Chinook = if_else(Chinook == "I", "1", Chinook)) %>% 
  mutate(Chinook = as.numeric(Chinook)) %>% 
  pivot_longer(-c(Region, Year), 
               names_to = "species", 
               values_to = "catch") %>%
  mutate(catch = catch * 1000) %>% 
  group_by(Region) %>% 
  summarize(mean_catch = mean(catch)) %>% 
  arrange(desc(mean_catch))
```

---

## {#pipeline-as-narrative data-menu-title="Pipeline as Narrative"}

[Reading the Pipeline as a Narrative]{.slide-title}

:::{.body-text}
Each line is an **analytical decision**:

1. Remove irrelevant columns
2. Fix a known data entry error
3. Convert the fixed column to numeric
4. Reshape to long format for analysis
5. Convert units to actual fish counts
6. Group by region
7. Calculate mean catch per region
8. Sort to see the highest-catch regions first

The code **documents your reasoning** — not just what you did, 
but in what order and why each step follows from the last.
:::
